Okay. The video was visually appealing, and I enjoyed watching it even though I disagree with its central premise. Now I'm hungry too. The main idea of this video is that there are several government programs that Donald Trump would like to cut, and they shouldn't be cut because they only cost you a few dollars per year.

I could bring out the old "this stuff should be cut because it's not the purpose of the government," but I'm sure my audience has heard that already, so I will focus on the details instead of the theme of small government.

One of things I thought of right away is that he's only looking at the costs, while simply assuming the benefits merit spending this sum of money. He's just saying, "This stuff is cheap, so why not pay for it?" By this logic, I should head to the thrift store and buy some women's pants and toys. I'm not a woman and I don't have kids, but hey, it's cheap so it must be worth it. Are these government programs really doing that much to help people? This is something that must be investigated.

Statist thinking encourages you to look at the benefits while ignoring the costs. "Look at all the jobs our infrastructure program created! And now we have all these shiny new bridges!" Yes, but someone had to pay for that. How much money was spent (even wasted) in the process? Did the increase in taxes to fund the bridges cause jobs across the private sector to be lost because taxation is bad for the economy? How many people in our town can't afford some good or service because they were forced to pay a tax? The fallacious logic here is that because there are significant benefits, it must be worth it. I think the guy here is doing the opposite. His logic is that the costs are low, so it must be worth it.

We can also refute his argument that the costs of these government programs are low. Billions are being poured into them. He just makes it look like a little bit by dividing it by the number of people in the country. But think of the things that private citizens could have done if they collectively had Billions more in wealth.

If this money stayed in private hands, would it have done anything better? Probably, since government spends money indiscriminately while individuals carefully allocate their funds in order to maximize their satisfaction.

Now let's go for the kill shot. If these programs (public broadcasting, funding for the arts, supporting minority-owned businesses, spouting climate alarmism, etc.) were really that useful to people, then they would find ways to fund them voluntarily. So there's no reason to force people to pay for them. If this money is being allocated in such a manner as to bring maximum satisfaction to every single taxpayer who's being forced to fund this, then why not have a government program to fund it? But if not, people are being forced to misallocate resources that could be put towards better things.
